elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted clause: "Corio may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". Corio is the Customer. The Agreement has no Order Form or partial-termination structure, so covering "this Agreement" is the full scope available, and omitting "in whole or in part" is correct surplus avoidance.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly 30 days, in writing, no additional conditions or approval requirement attached.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall refund to Corio, pro rata, any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination" — the words "pro rata" are express, not merely inferred from post-termination coverage, and the refund obligation runs from Vendor to Customer.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." Retained §11.2 gives Vendor only breach/insolvency exits; the §11.1 either-party notice at least 30 days before expiration is natural-term non-renewal effective at expiration (a RENEWAL matter), not a mid-term convenience right, so it does not contradict the new bar.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The inserted notice period is thirty (30) days, which is outside the 60–90 day fallback band (it is the preferred, more Customer-favourable figure).

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither the retained §§11.1–11.2 nor the insertion imposes any early-termination fee, penalty, instalment acceleration or contingent payment on Corio, so there is no fee requiring a cap.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Satisfied a fortiori: the insertion bars Commerce One from any convenience termination during the initial or any renewal term, leaving only §11.1 non-renewal effective at expiration of the then-current term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: No 90-day Vendor notice appears; the only Vendor exit-on-notice mechanic left is the §11.1 non-renewal notice of 30 days prior to expiration. Vacuous satisfaction is unavailable because §11.1 still permits Vendor to end the relationship on 30 days' notice at term end (a RENEWAL issue, but it means no 90-day figure exists here).

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete: all four preferred elements are met in operative language (30 days' written notice, express pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during the initial and renewal terms).

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present" returning false is a naming artefact, not a substantive gap: the checker matches generic aliases (Customer/Client/Licensee) while the inserted clause names the actual Customer party, "Corio". Substantively the rendered text plainly grants Corio a convenience right.

Minimality holds: a single concise insertion for a genuinely missing clause; §§11.1 and 11.2 are retained verbatim, no words outside the checklist were deleted, and no extras (survival tail, at-own-expense language, notice procedures, damages carve-outs, or "in whole or in part") were added — correct given there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure.

Intent is preserved: the breach and insolvency exits, the Software-specification material-condition sentence, and the §11.1 term/auto-renewal mechanics all survive without contradiction; no undefined term or dangling cross-reference is created.

Drafting nit to repair (not an element failure): the new paragraph is rendered as an unnumbered "Termination for Convenience." heading while §§11.1–11.2 are numbered, and the rationale/comment refer to "§ 11.3". Number the insertion "11.3" so the section citation in the comment matches the operative text.

Fallback is not independently complete (30-day Customer notice is outside the 60–90 band and no 90-day Vendor notice figure exists), but that is immaterial because the preferred level is fully met; the comment appropriately offers the fallback as a negotiating step without conceding it in the operative text.
